title: Physics-informed quantum algorithms for glueball-like excitations in a $\mathbb{Z}_2$ lattice gauge theory
abstract: Glueball spectroscopy with quantum computing requires both a correlated gauge vacuum and a systematic construction of its low-lying pure-gauge excitations. We develop a physics-informed quantum-computing framework for these tasks in a $(2+1)$-dimensional $\mathbb{Z}_2$ lattice gauge theory. We use the term \emph{glueball-like} for localized closed-flux excitations on the confining side of this Abelian model, without identifying them with the non-Abelian glueballs of QCD. The central strategy is to organize the computation around the physical structure of the glueball-like state rather than to search a generic many-body excitation space. We prepare the gauge vacuum variationally and use Wilson-loop quantum subspace expansion to construct and characterize the low-lying excitations. Moreover, eigenvector continuation uses nearby ground states to capture the growing loop dressing without a rapidly enlarged Wilson-loop basis, while a Bethe--Salpeter-type radius quantifies the associated spatial broadening. We further use quench dynamics to probe nonequilibrium production. Although demonstrated in an Abelian model, the framework is built from gauge-invariant vacuum and excitation structures and is naturally transferable to non-Abelian lattice gauge theories.
summary: This work introduces a physics-informed quantum algorithm to study glueball-like excitations in a Z2 lattice gauge theory. It uses variational quantum circuits and Wilson-loop expansions to calculate the excitation spectrum and spatial size of these excitations. The approach is valuable because it systematically incorporates physical symmetries and structure, making it transferable to more complex, non-Abelian gauge theories.
main_problem: The paper develops a physics-informed quantum-computing framework to study glueball-like excitations in a lattice gauge theory.
main_result: The framework successfully characterizes the low-lying excitation spectrum and the spatial profile of these excitations by projecting the Hamiltonian onto a gauge-invariant subspace.
method: It employs a combination of variational quantum circuits for vacuum preparation, Wilson-loop quantum subspace expansion (QSE) for excitations, and eigenvector continuation for basis compression.
model_or_system: The study is performed on a (2+1)-dimensional Z2 lattice gauge theory, governed by a Hamiltonian involving magnetic and electric plaquette terms. The physical states must satisfy Gauss's law.
key_observables: Glueball-like excitation energy spectrum, Bethe-Salpeter (BS)-type radius quantifying spatial broadening, and quench observables $N_K(t)$.
important_parameters: The coupling parameter $x$ controls the transition between confined ($x > x_c$) and deconfined ($x < x_c$) regimes, with $x_c \simeq 0.2473$.
main_assumptions: The framework is demonstrated in an Abelian model but is claimed to be naturally transferable to non-Abelian lattice gauge theories. The QSE basis size is limited by the maximum loop size considered.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the workflow, showing vacuum preparation via loop-gas circuits refined by variational layers, and visualizing how Wilson-loop excitations define a nonorthogonal subspace for state calculation.
paper_structure: The paper proceeds by defining the physical problem in the Z2 lattice gauge theory, developing the physics-informed quantum framework (vacuum preparation and excitation construction), and then applying this to calculate spectral properties and spatial profiles using BS-radius and quench dynamics.
why_interesting: The methodology—using physical structure (gauge invariance, loop operators) to constrain the quantum computational basis—is a powerful paradigm for applying quantum algorithms to strongly correlated lattice models, which is highly relevant to quantum simulation.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Algorithmic workflow. (a) Rotated representation of the Z2 gauge model. Contractible products of magnetic pla- quettes generate closed-flux loops on a vacuum. (b) Vacuum preparation starts from the loop-gas circuit V (θ) and is re- fined by gauge-preserving variational layers. (c) Wilson-loop excitations define a nonorthogonal subspace in which low- lying glueball-like states and their observables are obtained from measured overlap and Hamiltonian matrices.

FIG. 2. Vacuum preparation on the 6 × 4 periodic lattice. Left (a and b): comparison of the one-parameter loop-gas ansatz with exact diagonalization over the interpolation parameter x. Right(c and d): HVA refinement at the representative point x = 0.2. The variational energy approaches the exact value and the state infidelity decreases with layer number p. The two panels illustrate complementary roles: the loop gas captures the exactly solvable limits and much of the bulk trend, while the HVA repairs the intermediate-coupling correlations that the factorized plaquette coordinates cannot represent.

FIG. 3. Structure of the low-lying QSE states at x = 0.6. Left: coefficients associated with elementary-plaquette loop operators in a fixed QSE basis. Right: local elementary-loop motif density ⟨np⟩. The first excited state is spatially uniform in these diagnostics. The two higher states are degenerate within the reported precision; their individual coefficient patterns are therefore basis-dependent until a spatial symmetry is diagonalized inside the degenerate subspace. Choosing reflection eigenstates produces the displayed even/odd patterns (P = ±1), while the motif density provides a basis-independent view of their spatial support.

FIG. 4. Subspace compression. (a) energy errors of the three lowest glueball-like excitations decrease as the largest Wilson-loop area np is increased. (b) vacuum-only EC for the first excitation, using the training set {x −0.05C, . . . , x, . . . , x + 0.05C} with C = 1, 2, 3. (c) combined EC and loop bases for the two lowest excitations of the target Hamiltonian at x = 0.4. The available training vacua are sampled on the grid x = 0.05, 0.10, . . . , 0.70, and C enlarges the selected training set. The labels 0p, 1p, and 2p denote the three loop-basis choices used in the data, with loop-size cutoffs np = 0, 1, 2, respectively.

FIG. 6. Production of bare closed-loop motifs after quenches from the electric vacuum at x0 = 1 to x1 = 0.1 and x1 = 0.6. The curves correspond to four loop shapes, denoted L1, L2, L3, and Λ in the original numerical data. The deep quench to x1 = 0.1 generates substantially more loop weight, including larger motifs, whereas the x1 = 0.6 quench remains electric- field dominated and suppresses extended loops.
